y1-life.name: Life Imagined

y1-audiovisual.name: Introduction to Audiovisual Arts
y1-audiovisual.content:
This course introduces you to foundational features of the audiovisual and performing arts worlds. It focuses upon the critical and prominent role that film (and television), music, theatre, performing arts, and video play in an increasingly interactive and global arts environment. During the course, we explore relevant historical cases as well as more recent
transformations in relation to the arts. Examples highlight art forms in which their respective technologies interact and where audio and visual aspects intersect. Further, we explore ways in which different media impact the production and reception of artworks and their related artistic practices. In analysing these examples, we draw on prominent
theoretical concepts supported by a cultural studies framework. Ultimately, this course equips you with a basic knowledge of contemporary and emerging art forms along with historical and theoretical knowledge about theatre, music, film, and other audiovisual and performing arts. In the first half of this course, we focus upon comprehension of foundational facets and key concepts of the audiovisual arts. The second half of the course expands various conceptual and methodological frameworks and applies them to relevant audiovisual artforms and media. Throughout the course, students will be exposed to cases drawn from fictional and
documentary films, music videos and recordings, sound installations, theatre, performance, television, and digital culture.

Course Objectives
- Differentiate between various art forms and media in order to variously interpret their creative, cultural, and aesthetic value
- Grasp and summarize core concepts from film, music, theatre and performing arts theory
- Recognize these concepts’ relations and applications to contemporary audiovisual media and culture
- Through written work and discussion, identify a corpus of important audiovisual and performing works from the twentieth century to the present
- Grasp and summarize core arguments from course readings
- In written and oral form, articulate an argument in relation to relevant artworks drawing from core theoretical concepts from the course

y1-sociology.name: Sociology of the Arts
y1-sociology.content:
Sociology of the Arts is an introduction for students into how sociologists study the arts. The course starts with a presentation of the field of research, the core questions that this field of research deals with and the way in which sociologists define what art is based on the institutionalisation of art or the function of art. Then, the course turns attention to what sociology is, to how sociologists tend to do research, and to how different theoretical strands exist within sociology: critical sociology, interpretative value sociology and social systems theory. 
Subsequently, the course focuses on two of these strands of art sociological research: critical theories and interpretative value sociology. The most important art sociological theories in each strand are introduced and the benefits and shortcomings of each of them are discussed. Through empirical examples students learn how to use the key concepts of the theories. We start with distinction theory and field theory (and its elaborations in studies of the creative industries) as they have been developed by Pierre Bourdieu and criticize these theories through more recent empirical studies of cultural tastes and artistic careers. Then, the art world theory of Howard Becker, and Actor-Network theory – that adds the relevance of objects and technologies in understanding social relations in and around the arts – are introduced. 
The course ends by analysing examples of art policies studies using the perspective of pragmatic sociology that provides a bridge between the critical and interpretative perspectives. Lastly, the course focuses on the relevance of studying the aesthetic features of art works which helps developing a sociology of art that is truly about art.

y1-impact.name: Stories We Live By: Mediating Identities
y1-impact.entry:
This module is open for:
* students of the BA American Studies
* students of the BA Arts, Culture and Media
* students of the BA Communication Science
* students of the BA Dutch Language and Culture
* students of the BA English Language and Culture
* students of the BA European Languages and Cultures
* students of the BA Media Studies
* exchange students at the Faculty of Arts
y1-impact.content:
Stories are more than just communication tools. They are social and cultural constructs that shape how we understand ourselves and the world around us. Drawing from literary studies, linguistics, media and cultural studies, this interdisciplinary course explores questions relating
to narrative and identity in different media formats (e.g. novels, speeches, films, news, songs, video games, social media, and everyday conversations). More specifically, the course will offer students an introduction to the elementary mechanics of discourse, storytelling and narrative, their linguistic elements and media formats as well as their effects in specific realms of everyday life.

Two weekly interactive lectures will offer students a combination of introductions to theoretical and formal concepts as well as applied case study narratives based on the key “stories” that can be seen to define our present day realities. Concepts may include: discourse, framing, metaphor, ideology, identity and points of view, sequencing, focalisation, character, genre/ media formats, symbolism, encoding/decoding, audiences, othering. Case study narratives may come from the
following thematic clusters: planetary crisis, fake news and propaganda, migrants and refugees, sex vs. gender, democracy and its discontents, health and illness, foundational myths and cultural memory, ‘the west and the rest’, protagonists/ antagonists, neoliberal capitalism, stories of conflict and reconciliation. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of theories of identity, belonging and cultural memory in literary, (socio) linguistic and media theories and how the format in which these stories are told play a role.
Topics in any given year may vary depending on the specific expertise of staff teaching the course.

y1-film.name: Film I: Film Analysis
y1-film.content:
This course introduces film as an art form. Students will be familiarized with the medium of film, the principles and techniques by which films tell stories and visualize their characters and storyworlds, basic theoretical concepts, and the terminological apparatus of film studies. Offering both theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for analyzing moving images, the course revolves around the following concepts: film form, narrative form, visual storytelling, frames and framing, focalization, and film art. Each concept is illustrated by a specific, closely related genre, and the screenings broaden the scope of the analytical category.
This course primarily designed to help students acquire basic analytical tools, concepts, and technical aspects of cinema. In this context, ‘analysis’ means the search for meaning in the interaction with a film, where ‘meaning’ is not understood as an inherent property but an effect created by and resulting from viewers’ engagement. The primary aim of the course is therefore to explain how films encourage viewers to perform analytical activities, how they guide our understanding, and why and how moving images produce certain effects.

y1-music.name: Music I: Introduction to Music Studies
y1-music.content:
The first half of this course is an introduction to general musical concepts, which are illustrated primarily  with examples from classical music. The second half continues this introduction but in reference to popular music forms and styles from early blues to recent genres like SoundCloud rap and hyperpop. The course does not require any prior knowledge of music notation or music  theory.
The first half treats questions like: what is (classical) music, what is music history, what is a composition or musical work, what is musicology and what are its  traditions and methodologies, how do we use music (actively and passively), can music have  meaning, and what is the impact of recording technology? The seminars in the first half will feature an  introduction to basics of music terminology, combined with exercises to recognize simple  musical structures aurally. 
The second half provides students the basic analytical tools to understand the cultural, musical and theoretical history of popular music. Students develop listening skills that will help them make connections and divisions between various popular genres in a historical framework. Students also develop a basic musicological understanding of song forms, instrumental textures, and histories of popular music technologies. Students acquire a critical vocabulary which enables them to examine the ideological and cultural motivations for musical creation and consumption.

y2-film-history.name: Film II: Film History
y2-film-history.entry:
Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA. 
Students must have passed LWX043P10 Film I: Film Analysis (or the earlier LWX019P05 Film 1a and LWX020P05 Film Ib).
Please note: this prerequisite does not apply to students who take this course as part of the faculty minor Film and Contemporary Audiovisual Media.
y2-film-history.content:
This course offers an overview of the history of film from the 1890s until today. It deals with the most important periods, modes, styles, and genres in film history. In addition, we will not forget the rise of television, video, and digital media and the resulting interplay between the different media. Although the focus will be on the development of fiction film, we will also devote attention to such filmic modes as experimental film and documentary. 

This film course is accompanied by a series of ten film screenings in an actual cinema, which are preceded by a 10-15 minute introduction. The screenings take place on Wednesday between 11.00am and ca. 1.45pm in the Forum Groningen (Nieuwe Markt 1).

Note that it is a necessary part of studying film to watch a wide range of movies in their proper cinematic surroundings. Hence attending the screenings will be an obligatory part of the course! We therefore highly recommend to reserve the time slot in your schedules.

y2-music-history.name: Music II: History and Theory of Classical Music
y2-music-history.entry:
Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA. 
Students must have passed LWX044P10 Music Analysis (or the earlier LWX023P05 Music 1a and LWX024P05 Music 1b).
Please note: this prerequisite does not apply to students who take this course as part of the faculty minor Arts & Culture: Music, Theatre and Performance Studies.
y2-music-history.content: The aim of this course is to acquaint students with the major developments in the history of Western art music while also surveying current debates concerning the various methods applied to the study of classical music. The course will also address the relevance of these debates for contemporary, performance and music life. Finally, this course seeks to deepen insight into the formal attributes of classical music works through listening assignments. The course does not require knowledge of music theory or music notation.

y2-mediality.name: Mediality to Intermediality
y2-mediality.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-mediality.content:
We live in a mediatized world, surrounded by and participating in media. Media constitute contemporary culture, rather than merely representing it. With the increasing impact of digitalization, the linkages between different media have intensified.

Similarly, the arts seem to have become increasingly multi-medial. Through forms such as digital screens, performance spaces, film, or interactive apps it is obvious that media and the arts are intrinsically interrelated. 

In this course, we will critically examine the changing interrelations of various media and artforms in contemporary culture. We will consider the connections and interactions among media in the arts (music, literature, theater, fine arts and film). The first block will begin with a historical perspective, reading classic texts on the arts to examine conceptions and comparisons of arts and media. The second block will focus on contemporary theories of media culture, inter- and transmediality. Students will be trained to apply these insights to case analyses.

y2-impact.name: Stories We Live By: Narrating the World
y2-impact.entry:
This module is open for: 
- students with a positive BSA from all BA programmes at the Faculty of Arts (*)
(*) The following BA programmes do not take part in 2026-2027:
Dutch Languages and Cultures; History; Linguistics.
y2-impact.content:
This course provides students with resources and (digital) tools to appreciate and produce narratives. Students will engage in theoretical and reflexive discussions about the nature of storytelling and its embedded discourses and ideologies, and are invited to reflect on the role that narratives and storytelling can have in tackling societal challenges such as migration, inequality, inclusivity and climate change. Interactive lectures at the beginning of the course will provide students with various frameworks and methodologies with which we can approach the most pressing narratives of the world in, ideally and specifically, a multi- or even interdisciplinary manner. Tutorials - in which students work in teams, preferably representing multiple disciplinary backgrounds - will then invite students to put these theoretical
considerations to the test and into practice. They will create publicly engaging outputs (in different media) that reflect their disciplinary training as critical citizens who are trained in the Humanities but also show an outward multi- and interdisciplinary perspective.

From the beginning of the course, students will be guided, step-by-step, from idea(s) to concrete output in textual, audio and (audio-)visual media. The step-by-step guidance will include:
* Identification and analysis of a problematic discourses in this world (e.g. girls are not good at sports, the climate crisis is a hoax, migrants are a drain on the economy, school/university education does not prepare graduates for the real world; multilingualism creates barriers);
* conceiving of a potential societal partner (e.g., an NGO, museum, commercial business) and designing and creating a counter narrative;
* identification of an appropriate medium for distributing the counter discourse (i.e. a podcast, social media campaign, short documentary
film); producing a final product.

y2-film-theory.name: Film III: Film Theory
y2-film-theory.entry:
Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA. 
Students must have passed LWX001B10 Film II: Film History.
y2-film-theory.content:
The objective of this course is to provide students with an understanding of the theoretical, conceptual and methodological tools used to frame film and media research. “Nothing is more practical than a good theory,” as the saying goes. Therefore, the lectures will offer an overview of the most important film theories. In the seminars, we will discuss the key texts, steering paradigms, basic assumptions, and key concepts that have shaped the field of film and media theory. 

The different phases and theoretical paradigms to be examined in this course are (among others): Theories of Realism; Russian Formalism and Constructivism; Apparatus Theory; Feminist Film Theory; Cognitive Film Theory; (Experimental) Media Archaeology; Sound Theories; Postcolonial Theory;  Film-Phenomenology, Theories of Bodies and Affects.

We will read texts by canonical film and media theorists such as Hugo Münsterberg, Sergei Eisenstein, Siegfried Kracauer, André Bazin, Laura Mulvey, Linda Williams, Michel Chion and Vivian Sobchack.

Film viewings form a mandatory part of this course.

y2-narrativity.name: Narrativity Across Media
y2-narrativity.entry:
Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA. 
Students must have passed LWX042P10 Life Imagined.
y2-narrativity.content:
Stories are everywhere: in our everyday exchanges, in the journalistic media, in religion, philosophy, law, medicine, management, in the sciences, and – prominently– in the arts: in literature, theatre, or film, clearly, but in paintings and music too. 

Underlying this diversity of stories seems to be an innate narrative capacity: a cognitive predisposition of humans to narrativity. Narratives allow individuals and communities to give form to (and reflect on) their experiences, their values, their history, and their sense of identity. 

This course teaches you to analyse the forms and functions of narrative and storytelling across art forms. How do literature, film, music, theatre, or paintings tell stories? What conventions and cognitive abilities underlie our perception of narrativity in art? And how do various media cooperate in conveying stories? 

While the first half of the course addresses these questions theoretically, the second half has students collaborate on creative projects of their own. In small teams, students gain experience in project management by creating an interactive story (or storyworld) that spreads across different media, applying the acquired theoretical knowledge of block 1 in relation to interacting (and interactive) media.

y2-studio.name: From Studio to Exhibition
y2-studio.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-studio.content: From Studio to Exhibition: Practices and Publics in Contemporary Art offers a survey of contemporary art from the 1990s to the present. The history of contemporary art contains a tapestry of stories. Rather than following a strict chronological, geographical, or stylistic line, the course is structured by recurring and often debated topics revolving around Memory, Identity, Placement, Digitization. Attention will be paid to the institutional, social and political contexts in which contemporary art developed, as well as to developments in the infrastructure and functioning of Art Worlds. By studying the biography of artworks, we will explore life cycles and trajectories of works of art, from studio to exhibition and beyond. The course provides tools to critically analyze and reflect on the art (world) of today.

y3-practice.name: Arts in Practice
y3-practice.entry:
Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
Depending on the specialization, students must have past the Arts Discipline III course.
y3-practice.content: 'Arts in Practice' applies the skills and theoretical insights gained in the preceding four arts courses. Students use their acquired knowledge to creatively engage with and advance the current status of the professional arts sector. They do this in relation to their chosen arts profession profile. Throughout the semester, students actively participate in both theoretical reflection and hands-on experience in the field. This can be accomplished by cooperating in the organization of a music festival, creating video essays, or developing a theatre performance.

y3-thesis.name: BA thesis in Arts, Culture and Media
y3-thesis.entry:
Second year completed.
NB.: This requirement does not apply for taking part in the thesis preparation during the first semester of the third year and the workshops during the first weeks of the second semester of the third year.
y3-thesis.content:
To become a Bachelor of Arts, Culture and Media, each student writes a Bachelor Thesis. The thesis demonstrates expert knowledge according to the specialisation: Arts, Policy and Management (APCE) or Arts and Criticism (A&C) and the art discipline(s) the student has chosen. 

The thesis will typically be written in Semester II, block B, but can in exceptional cases also be written in Semester I. At the start of the second semester (February), there will be a lecture providing guidelines regarding the thesis pocess. Students develop a topic and research proposal in block IIa (February-March). After approval of the thesis proposal the student writes the thesis supervised by a staff member in block IIb.

Strict deadlines apply for handing in assignments, the thesis proposal and the concept and final version of the thesis. this is necessary to properly organize the thesis process and in order to provide students with the documents necessary for applying for a master programme per September of the new academic year.

y3-evaluating.name: Evaluating the Arts
y3-evaluating.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y3-evaluating.content: This course looks directly to the contemporary and recent historical field of arts criticism. Here students examine both respected and prolific arts critics in the fields of journalism and professional arts worlds with subjects taken literature, film, music and theater criticism. By reading both shorter exposés such as the record or concert review to the film and theater performance review, students begin to recognize the pithy, poetic, yet functional language of arts criticism intended for a broader public. In the second half of this course, students undertake their own arts criticism project which may take the form of an online blog reviewing various artistic examples from the student's chosen arts discipline such as music, film, theatre, visual art, or literature or may take the form of a video review channel composed of a set of video reviews that cohere in style, content, and negotiation of one's own personal critical voice.

y3-seminar.name: Advanced Seminar Theatre/Music/Film
y3-seminar.entry:
Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
Depending on the specialization, students must have past the Arts Discipline III course.
y3-seminar.content: This course is the culmination of the arts disciplinary path students develop in Arts, Culture, and Media and it guides students through advanced investigation and discussion of academic literature in their chosen arts discipline (music, theatre, or film). Students deepen their knowledge of that literature and core theoretical frameworks and methdological approaches in that literature, which they use in the preparation of their own original arts research project/paper.

reconciliation: Part B lists LFW004B10 beside Stories We Live By: Narrating the World, but the dated Ocasys group and individual catalogue identify that title as LFW002B10. LFW004B10 is instead Cultural Heritage. Retain the first-listed title and use its verified catalogue code.

Music II has a stale Ocasys reference to Music Analysis. Part B Article 7.1 requires the corresponding first discipline course, and Article 8.1 identifies the older Music Analysis course as the equivalent predecessor. The regular entrant completes Music I in year one.
progression: First year 30 EC in each semester. Complete the first year and obtain positive study advice before higher-year coursework. Film I and Music I precede Film II and Music II.

Year two first semester is Film II, Music II and Mediality to Intermediality. Second semester is the faculty-wide narrative course and 20 EC from the listed group. Film II precedes Film III. Life Imagined precedes Narrativity Across Media. Film III is the discipline prerequisite for the film seminar and Arts in Practice.

Year three places the 30 EC minor or study abroad first. Approved choice is left generic. The final semester contains practice, evaluation, the film seminar and thesis. The thesis requires completion of the second year before writing. Earlier preparation and workshops are explicitly exempt.
